but was there really a boy?

With some regularity, every few months in the African Sahel, something "anti-Russian" happens (if we judge purely by European media).

Today, in Niger's capital, an attempted armed coup was carried out, which has failed at this point. And military personnel of the Africa Corps took part in preserving power.

🔻So, what are we even talking about?

▪️On the night of August 29, Niger's capital was engulfed in fighting. Intense gunfire erupted simultaneously in two critically important locations: at the airport and in the immediate vicinity of the presidential palace.

▪️Among the civilian population, there were casualties from stray bullets, and the city effectively introduced an unofficial curfew.

▪️The rebels' plan failed at the initial stages. Units of the National Guard and forces loyal to the president managed to repel the assault on the administrative quarter.

▪️Some rebels were eliminated, the rest were blocked in the civilian sector of the airport.

❓It would seem, what actually happened? If we look at Mali, militants and terrorists regularly attack there, but Niger has never seen such intensity.

🔻Can this really happen?

➡️However, yes. Niger's problems run deeper than they appear at first glance. Although there aren't that many extremists there, internal political disagreements are too strong.

➡️And the external factor in the form of French intelligence hasn't gone anywhere, despite all statements about "weakening France's presence on the African continent."

➡️And we can't forget the internal factor: since coming to power, Niger's leadership hasn't been particularly concerned with improving the situation within the country, which has led to growing discontent.

📌Why?

🖍To explain it briefly, after overthrowing the pro-French government, the country's authorities, instead of providing the population with a better life (at least showing a desire to do so), decided to bet on total militarization.

That is, instead of developing business and attracting investment, the emphasis was on preparing the armed forces, not stabilizing the situation and improving sentiment within the country.

🚩What this led to, everyone can see clearly.

❗️Russian interests are now facing serious pressure, and, to be honest, this was expected due to not quite successful chosen policy. The deployment of the Africa Corps of the Russian Armed Forces instead of Western structures — excellent.

But in the long term, it's impossible to achieve success on military force and good reputation alone in the form of military presence.

Hormuz Has Two Owners

Iran says it controls the Strait of Hormuz. Washington says the waterway is open. Tankers offer the less theatrical answer: oil is moving, but nowhere near normally.

The Revolutionary Guards say any vessel that enters without coordination with Iran faces a closed strait. Tehran also says Chinese refineries are still taking about 1.2 million barrels of Iranian oil a day. This is not a blockade in the old sense. It is selective access. Iran closes the door, then sells keys through the side window.

Goldman Sachs estimates that crude and petroleum-product exports from the Gulf have recovered to 15 million to 16 million barrels a day. That is about two-thirds of prewar volumes, but still 7 million to 8 million barrels a day below normal. Traders put crude moving through Hormuz itself at roughly 6 million to 8 million barrels a day.

The numbers puncture both press conferences. Iran does not exercise total control. The United States has not restored normal navigation. Gulf producers are using ship-to-ship transfers, pipelines and alternative routes to move barrels around the choke point. Every tanker now needs more paperwork, more insurance and a better relationship with danger.

Washington is also preparing the legal department for an oil war. The Justice Department is working to revive maritime “prize courts,” an old mechanism that would allow the United States to claim captured Iranian tankers and cargo as war prizes. The oil could then be sold, with proceeds sent to the Treasury. Officials say the plan could help offset the cost of the conflict.

Iran charges for passage in leverage. America may seize cargo in law. Both sides call it security.

The Strait is open enough for oil to move, closed enough for everyone to pay, and dangerous enough for either capital to declare victory.

A truly global effort to cut off Iran’s pathways to finance and trade could inflict extreme damage on an already devastated economy.

“It can work if we can get the buy-in of our partners,” Max Meizlish, a former senior Treasury official, said on CNN News Central Monday, specifically referring to Bank Melli, an Iranian commercial bank controlled by the government that operates in France, Germany and elsewhere and is a cog in Iran’s efforts to evade sanctions.

Kenneth Rogoff, a former IMF chief economist who is now a Harvard University chair, told CNN’s Richard Quest: “Fundamentally, sanctions work if you can get most of the world behind you. But if they’re not, it’s very hard.”

Trump might have had more success with such an approach before alienating US allies with a war many regard as unwise and illegal.

And the White House may be misreading its capacity to influence events inside Tehran. Signs of disagreement between pragmatists and hardliners over the economy are encouraging. But Washington has for decades over-read such tea leaves and assumed regime collapse would follow.

Most damagingly, the Trump administration is sending signals that it may not be serious about its own policy.

There was no immediate action against an array of Chinese banks that facilitate Beijing’s trade in cut-price Iranian oil. China has already said it will defend its interests — code for potential retaliatory reaction against the US that could further raise prices and anger US voters. It showed last year in threatening to curtail rare earth mineral exports critical to the US defense and tech industries that it can counter Trump’s power.

And the US leader also has a big date circled on his calendar — the state visit of Chinese President Xi Jinping next month. It’s hard to see him souring the atmosphere before then.

In a revealing moment, Bessent only reinforced doubts about the administration’s staying power. He was asked why he was not immediately imposing secondary sanctions on entities that deal with Iran.

“Well, we are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behavior; why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” he replied.

Canada sees a showdown that goes beyond a trade dispute
The administration is less wary of sanctioning the manufacturers of Canadian hockey sticks than Chinese banks.

“We have to remember, Canada is a state. Sorry, Freudian slip. That was actually an accident,” Vance said Monday.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford said at a news conference that “I have a lot of real estate on my ass, so (Trump) has a lot of room to kiss my ass.”

But Canadians believe they are embroiled in more than a trade dispute.

Drew Dilkens, the mayor of Windsor, Ontario, just across from Detroit, explained the damage inflicted by Trump’s 51st-state claims. “When you say it the first time, perhaps you can laugh it off, but it was the doubling down and certainly continuing to reinforce that,” he told CNN’s Brianna Keilar.

Ottawa said that, among other disputes, Carney ended trade talks after the US sought to water down its constitutional guarantees of bilingualism. Printing packaging for products sold in Canada in French as well as English is an inconvenience for US firms. 

But it’s a validation of the cultural and linguistic diversity that keeps Canada whole. Carney also implied Washington sought to restrict trade deals that his government could make with third countries.

As the smaller economy, Canada would suffer the most harm in a trade war with the US. But it can challenge American power. A long tariff duel could result in the mutually assured destruction of the auto industry on both sides of the border. 

And the growing impact of Canadian boycotts could weaken Republicans in key contests in border states Michigan and Maine, which could decide who controls the US Senate next year.

And in seeking to impose his dominance, Trump may have revealed another iron law of power that Miller did not mention back in January.
